Great—have fun at the music store! Based on what you and I discussed earlier about Stratocasters and Les Pauls and getting good tone in alternate tunings, here are practical things to check when shopping:

- Match the guitar to the music you play. Les Paul–type guitars were described as staples for rock and blues (thick, sustaining tone); Strat-style guitars are more contoured and usually brighter. Think about the tonal character you want.
- Body and construction. Note differences in body shape and build: Strat-style instruments are contoured with a bolt-on neck; Les Pauls are single-cut, typically mahogany with a set-in neck and a carved top. These affect weight, feel, and tone.
- Neck and scale/playability. Try different neck profiles and scale lengths (the Strat example mentioned a 25.5" scale) to see what feels comfortable for your fretting and fingerstyle work.
- Pickups and electronics. Look for pickup types and features that give you the tones you want. Coil-tap/coil-splitting was mentioned as a useful option to expand tonal flexibility—useful if you want both thicker humbucker tones and brighter single-coil-like sounds.
- Suitability for fingerpicking/acoustic-like tones. If you plan to do delicate, acoustic-style fingerpicking (you asked about pieces like “Blackbird”), try the guitar unplugged and plugged in — some solid-body electrics can work, but feel and string spacing matter.
- Setup, strings, and tuning stability. For lower or alternate tunings (open D was discussed), heavier strings help; also check the guitar’s action and intonation and whether it’s easy to get adjusted in the shop. A good setup makes a big difference.
- Try multiple guitars. Play chords, single-note lines, and the styles you actually use (including fingerpicking and any tunings you’ll use) so you can compare feel and tone.
